title: Dirty Matcha: What It Is, What Is in It, and How It Differs From a Matcha Latte

seo.title: Dirty Matcha: What It Is vs. Matcha Latte
seo.meta_description: A dirty matcha combines matcha, milk, and coffee—usually espresso. A regular matcha latte has no coffee. The hybrid adds caffeine and roasted coffee flavor.
seo.search_intent: Understand what a dirty matcha is, which ingredients it usually contains, how it is assembled, and how it differs from a regular matcha latte.

excerpt: A dirty matcha is essentially a matcha latte with coffee added, usually one or two shots of espresso. It combines matcha's grassy, umami profile with roasted coffee notes. Because it contains both drinks, it also combines their caffeine contributions.
content_html:
A dirty matcha is essentially a matcha latte with coffee added, most often a shot of espresso. A standard matcha latte combines matcha, water, and milk; the “dirty” version adds coffee, creating a hybrid between tea and espresso drinks.

The term is not a legally standardized recipe. Some cafés use one espresso shot, others use two, and the proportions of matcha, milk, and sweetener vary widely. The defining feature is simply that both matcha and coffee are present.

What usually goes into a dirty matcha?

The common base is matcha dispersed in a small amount of water, milk or plant-based milk, and espresso. It can be served hot or iced and may be sweetened with sugar, honey, vanilla, or flavored syrup.

In iced versions, differences in liquid density allow green, white, and brown layers to remain visible for a while. Those layers are mainly presentation; they mix during drinking.

The difference from a matcha latte is the coffee

A regular matcha latte does not require espresso. Its flavor comes from powdered green tea and milk, creating a grassy, lightly bitter, sweet, and umami profile.

Dirty matcha adds the roasted, bitter, aromatic character of coffee. This can appeal to people who find a plain matcha latte too milky or want something closer to their usual espresso routine.

Caffeine changes too

Matcha already contains caffeine because it is powdered tea leaf. Adding espresso makes total caffeine roughly the contribution from both sources combined. There is no universal number because matcha dose, coffee variety, shot size, and number of shots vary.

For someone sensitive to caffeine, that means ordering a dirty matcha is more than a flavor change compared with a same-size matcha latte.

How do you make one at home?

First make a smooth matcha concentrate with sifted powder and a small amount of hot water. Prepare espresso separately. Add milk to the glass, ice for a cold version, and pour the two concentrates in whatever order gives the appearance you want.

If taste is the priority, order matters little after mixing. If visible layers matter, temperature, density, and pouring speed become more important.

Do matcha and espresso somehow cancel each other out?

No. Combining tea and coffee does not neutralize caffeine or create a reaction that removes its stimulant effect. They are simply two caffeine-containing ingredients in one drink.

Matcha contributes tea compounds while coffee contributes its own chemistry. That does not make the combination automatically healthy or unhealthy; it is simply a different beverage formulation.

Why is dirty matcha trending in 2026?

Google Trends identified “dirty matcha” as a breakout search during 2026 as part of a broader surge in customized matcha drinks. The trend fits a larger café pattern of combining familiar beverage categories and building visually layered drinks.

The appearance helps online too: dark espresso, pale milk, and vivid green matcha are immediately recognizable in photos and short videos.

There is no single dirty-matcha formula

Some cafés layer concentrated matcha and espresso over milk; others substitute cold brew for espresso or add vanilla, coconut, fruit, or flavored foam. The name is used fairly loosely as long as matcha and coffee both appear.

If caffeine or sugar intake matters to you, ask how many shots, how much matcha, and which syrups the specific recipe uses.

The practical rule: matcha latte equals matcha plus water and milk; dirty matcha is the same basic idea with coffee added. Expect a more roasted flavor and a higher, variable caffeine load.

As a practical reference, adjust only one variable afterward: tea amount, water amount, temperature, or whisking intensity. Changing everything at once makes it difficult to know what produced a smoother flavor, stronger cup, or better texture.

faq.question: What is in a dirty matcha?
faq.answer: Usually matcha, a small amount of water, milk, and one or more espresso shots; sweetener is optional.

faq.question: Is it the same as a matcha latte?
faq.answer: No. A matcha latte does not require coffee, while dirty matcha adds espresso or another coffee component.

faq.question: Does dirty matcha have more caffeine?
faq.answer: Usually yes because it combines caffeine from matcha with caffeine from coffee, although the exact total depends on the recipe.
